narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.2% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) for that year, well below the average of roughly the fifth or sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your first-year class rank was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. You again ranked in the second decile, far below the average sixth-decile performance of accepted students.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 35 it is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, and this relatively solid score helped push the prediction somewhat toward passing. However, it was not enough to overcome the negative impact of your two class-rank indicators.

The model therefore concluded that your overall academic trajectory pointed to an elevated chance of failing the bar. To improve your prospects, you should focus on raising your class standing in future years if possible, consider retaking the LSAT to boost that score further, and explore additional bar-preparation resources before reapplying.
